analysis.one_liner: Gives families an $800-per-child refundable tax credit and boosts the Earned Income Tax Credit, paid for by higher taxes on the wealthy.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote, despite 56 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the tax deduction for children with an $800 refundable credit per child — meaning even families who owe little or no income tax would get the money as a refund. It would have enlarged the Earned Income Tax Credit and let families receive those credits in quarterly cash payments during the year instead of one annual refund. To pay for it, the bill would have raised the top income tax rate to 35% and added an 11% surtax on incomes above roughly $125,000 to $250,000 depending on filing status.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families with children, especially low- and moderate-income families. The child credit is refundable, so families with little tax liability still receive the full amount as a refund. The larger Earned Income Tax Credit and new quarterly advance payments would put cash in working parents' pockets throughout the year rather than once a year at tax time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income working families with children

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable $800 tax credit for each child under 18, replacing the personal exemption deduction for children, and adjusts the credit for inflation [S2][S3].
Because the credit is refundable, families who owe little or no federal income tax still collect it, unlike a deduction which only helps those who owe tax [S2][S3].
Increases the Earned Income Tax Credit, phasing the higher percentages in over 1992 and 1993 — reaching a 32% credit rate for families with three or more children [S2][S3].

Requires the Treasury to make quarterly advance payments of the child credit and Earned Income Tax Credit to eligible families, with special procedures to make sure families with incomes of $12,000 or less actually receive the payments [S2][S3].

Pays for the family tax relief by raising the top individual rate to 35%, imposing an 11% surtax on incomes above $250,000 for joint filers (lower thresholds for others), raising the alternative minimum tax rate to 29%, and applying these to estates and trusts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with high adjusted gross income — above $250,000 on joint returns, $200,000 for heads of household, $150,000 for single filers, and $125,000 for married filers separately — through a new surtax and a 35% top rate, plus estates and trusts, which also face the higher rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the 35% top rate starting at fairly low income levels — $66,000 for single filers and $78,400 for joint filers under the proposed rate table — so the burden would fall partly on upper-middle-income earners, not only the very wealthy [S3].

Replacing the child personal exemption deduction with a flat credit would leave some higher-income families worse off, since a deduction for a child was worth more to a household in a high tax bracket than an $800 credit [S3].

At the same time it raises rates, the bill repeals the existing limits on itemized deductions and the phaseout of personal exemptions, which would cut taxes for some of the same high earners the surtax targets — complicating who actually gains and loses [S2][S3].

Quarterly advance payments require families to estimate their income a year ahead, and the bill lets Treasury adjust later payments when estimates change, which could create repayment headaches for families whose income rises mid-year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: cash tax relief for working families with children, financed by higher taxes on high incomes. The main honest objections are that the 35% rate starts at incomes many would call upper-middle-class rather than rich, and the bill simultaneously repeals limits on high earners' deductions, muddying its own redistributive goal. The advance-payment system adds administrative risk for families with unstable incomes. On balance the benefits to working families are large and the costs fall mainly above the top of the income scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it quietly died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Downey of New York introduced the Working Family Tax Relief Act of 1991 on May 7, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 56 cosponsors — 55 Democrats and 1 Independent — with additional sponsors added through October 1991, including future House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Bernie Sanders [S3][S4].
Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law, never reported the bill or scheduled any action on it [S5].
No floor vote ever took place in either chamber, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households came out ahead: they avoided the 35% top rate and the new surtax because the bill never advanced. Working families with children got no child credit and no larger Earned Income Tax Credit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households and their tax bills

for.name: Rep. Thomas J. Downey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: 55 of 267 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members added through October 1991.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the sole non-Democrat among its 56 cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral — no markup, no report, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Had negotiated the 1990 budget agreement that raised the top rate to 31% and strongly resisted returning to higher income tax rates on the wealthy; the administration was not supportive of repealing the 1986 rate structure.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republicans sponsored the bill, and the Democratic chairman of the tax-writing committee never brought it up.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 35% top rate, an 11% surtax above roughly $125,000–$250,000, and a higher minimum tax, with the revenue funding credits for working families. Because the bill died, these households paid nothing extra. It also would have repealed limits on their itemized deductions, partially offsetting the increases [S2][S3].

Quarterly advance payments of the child credit and Earned Income Tax Credit would have created new administrative work for employers and the Treasury, while giving families steadier cash flow. The mechanism resembles the existing advance-EIC system it would have replaced [S3].
